I hope we'll see parties in these ambitious outside groups using the spaces to listen to each other, as well as pushing forward agendas that matter to us all. In terms of leadership needed, I think we're looking at it. My friends, we need to be ready to take on the reins, to be bold and not to wait for others to step into the fray. There is work to be done at every level, and no one is going to do it for us. I hope we can continue to work together, support each other's initiatives, and keep pushing to deliver what our countries need. Como Tada, and I thank you.
Thank you. I now give the floor to Bernadette Arakuye, the Minister from Rwanda.

Thank you, Chair. I also want to begin by thanking the government of Panama and Vanuatu for convening this important dialogue. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Rwanda has always believed that we achieve more when we work together. We were proud to partner with Peru to propose the resolution that launched the negotiations for the global plastics treaty. We did so because no country can solve a global pollution crisis on its own. Gwanda had already taken strong national action to address plastic pollution. We banned plastic bags, restricted single use plastics, and worked hard to keep plastic waste out of our environment. But our experience also showed us that national action, while essential, cannot by itself address a pollution challenge of global scale. Plastic pollution is a shared challenge that requires shared solutions, common commitment, and effective multilateral action. That experience has shown us why multilateralism matters. At the same time, environmental multilateralism is under strain. reaching consensus is becoming more difficult, while the environmental challenges we face are becoming more urgent and severe. That is why it is precisely the wrong moment to retreat from cooperation. It is also the wrong time to fall into the trap of all or nothing thinking. We must continue to work through global frameworks, while also utilizing complementary coalitions and partnerships where countries are ready to move faster. The objective remains the same, bringing countries together and turning ambition into action. We can take confidence from the Montreal Protocol. It remains one of the strongest examples of what environmental multilateralism can achieve. Ten years ago, the Kigali Amendment to phase down dangerous HFCs was adopted. And in those 10 years, we have made significant progress. Our task now is to finish the job. Rwanda encourages remaining parties to ratify the Kigali Amendment and to help us achieve universal ratification. This November, we will welcome the world back to Kigali for MOP 38 and to celebrate 10 years of the amendment. I warmly invite you all to join us. And tomorrow, we will launch the Friends of the Kigali Amendment, a group of countries and parties and partners committed to its advancing implementation. I hope many of you will accept our friend request and join us in this endeavor as well. Excellencies, the challenge facing multilateralism are real, but they make cooperation more important and not less. And for Rwanda, the path forward is to make cooperation better and fairer and to keep moving together whenever and wherever progress is possible. Thank you.
Thank you, Minister. And I now call on Sigrid Asland, the Minister of Climate and Environment of Norway. You have the floor.

Thank you. I thank Panama and Vanuatu for the invitation to this event with such a pressing subject. I wanted to also join the club of small countries with big hearts that Panama launched. Multilateralism matters more today because of the nature of the challenges that we need to address. Multilateralism has also brought us immense and important results on many difficult issues. And then it is an exercise in coordination and collective action. And the principle is that when we act together, we achieve more than if we act alone. Consensus is a principle in environmental multilateralism, and I think no one here will disagree that it is not without its challenges. At its worst, it can result in outcomes that reflect the lowest common denominator and it may fail to deliver the action required to solve the problem. And in the past, we saw countries restrain themselves when consensus was the norm, wanting to go the extra mile to accommodate the concerns of the broad majority, and now it is different. The cost of saying no seems lower than ever to the extent that some countries are willing to block outcomes supported by a broad majority. So there is no question that we need to expand our toolbox, but we need to do so committed, I think, to the bedrock of multilateralism. And I wanted to put this in the context of the current plastics negotiations. Norway is proud to co-chair the High Ambition Coalition to End Plastic Pollution together with Rwanda. With 77 members from all over the world, we represent a significant share of the plastics market globally, and this treaty must set us on a path to indeed end plastic pollution. It is true that common standards, commitments to reduce waste, to handle chemicals, would shift markets and competition even with fewer countries. It is also true that for a treaty to actually be useful, it needs to be comprehensive, it needs to ensure change, it needs to provide results. And a treaty without this also has limited value. And so I know one could argue to go ahead with a coalition of the willing. I am concerned, however, that this would result in a proliferation of national, regional approaches, further increasing fragmentation on a very specific global problem. I therefore, and Norway remains, laser focused on achieving a most effective, comprehensive and accountable treaty in the spirit of multilateralism, remaining open to build on that. And Norway, therefore, remains committed to multilateralism, but also to keep exploring additional and complementary ways to collaborate on top of that. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much. And I now give the floor to Juan Miguel Cuna from the Philippines.

President, we'd like to thank also Panama and Vanuatu for the invitation tonight. Excellencies, distinguished delegates and colleagues. The central question before us is how environmental multilateralism can remain effective in a more difficult geopolitical environment.

Consensus is harder to achieve.

Negotiations are becoming more complex, and countries are expected to implement a growing number of commitments across climate change, biodiversity, pollution and other environmental issues. For many developing countries, These demands are not matched by comparable access to finance, technology, and capacity building. Fragmentation also remains a practical problem. Closely related environmental issues are addressed through separate institutions, reporting systems, and financing mechanisms. Renewal should therefore focus not only on new commitments, but on making the existing system easier to implement. reducing duplication, improving coordination, and directing more resources to delivery at the national level. International law has an important role. The ICJ advisory opinion on climate change provides greater clarity on the obligations of states under international law. But legal clarity has to be matched by the means to implement those obligations. For developing countries, access to finance, technology, and institutional capacity remains central to effective implementation. The plastics negotiations illustrate another difficulty. Agreement remains challenging on measures across the full life cycle of plastics, including product design, chemicals of concern, waste management, and financing. For the Philippines, an effective treaty must be ambitious but implementable, taking to account national circumstances and capabilities and provide adequate finance, technology transfer, and capacity building, particularly for developing countries. We also need better coordination across environmental agreements. Climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, land degradation, water stress, and pressures on marine ecosystems increasingly overlap. More compatible reporting systems, shared scientific information, coordinated technical assistance and better alignment of financing can reduce the burden on states without weakening existing treaty mandates. The same need for coordination applies to transboundary environmental harm. Shared waters, marine ecosystems, biodiversity corridors and transboundary pollution require practical arrangements for monitoring, information sharing and coordinated management. It also applies to crimes that affect the environment. wildlife trafficking, illegal logging, illegal mining, fisheries-related crime, and illegal waste movements can involve organized criminal networks, corruption, and illicit financial flows. Environmental agencies therefore need to work more closely with customs, law enforcement, prosecutors, and financial intelligence authorities, including through existing mechanisms under the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, where applicable. Renewing environmental multilateralism should ultimately mean a system that is easier to implement, less fragmented, and better to able respond to the way environmental problems actually arise. Thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you. I now give the floor to Krzysztof Balesta, Secretary of State, Ministry of Climate and Environment of Poland.

Thank you very much, Excellencies. Ladies and gentlemen, I took some notes and I don't want to repeat.

Statements of many of you who praise multilateralism. This is discussed without saying it's very much needed and we are in a crisis.

But let me try to give some recipes how we can do that, because today we live in a very, very challenging environment. And I think this makes our work so difficult. First thing is that it's not true that people stop caring about environment. It's certainly not true. It's that this unsecure world is priority number one for many people.

So security got most important for them.

And not only physical security, but economic security, the cost of living is going up, energy security.

We all see what's happening in the Strait of Hormuz.

So people really have different priorities.

But it doesn't mean that they stop caring about environment.

The second thing is that, and I blame myself as well, it's ever harder to explain to the people what we do at COPs. It's really, really difficult to explain what tangible results we bring back to our capitals and we bring.

Back to the people.

So if we lose the public, then there's a reverse spin and politicians get disinterested because the public's not interested, so why should we care? We're not going to be elected based on our multilateral engagement. So what can we change? What can we change? We have to work with what's on the table. Let's use the security angle. In Poland, we are investing in homegrown energy because it improves energy security, but it also reduces pollution. It's the same thing, but the focus is on energy security. Same goes for biodiversity and for climate adaptation. Investment in climate adaptation brings immediate results to the public. They feel that we do something for them. In terms of biodiversity, We are actually using nature as part of our shield on our external border. Some of you know that we share a border with an active ongoing war. So we using, we creating peatlands, we stop logging at the border, we let nature run its course and help us potentially defend ourselves. But it also has climate because it's carbon sequestration, it's biodiversity.

So let's use the new angle, the new.

World, and still care for the same principles that we used to do. Thank you very much.
Thank you. I now give the floor to Barbara Pompili, Ambassador for the Environment from France.

Thank you. Thank you, Chair. Minister, colleagues, friends, thanks Panama, Vanuatu, and all represented states for this discussion on such a complex yet crucial issue. Environmental action faces a cruel paradox. As the crisis intensifies, scientific consensus is questioned and ecological priorities are sidelined by competing crisis. We face a friction in parallel between the slow machinery of multilateral diplomacy and the urgent need for action. I agree with what my colleague just said. And yet, I would argue, this is precisely why multilateralism remains indispensable. It is still the only space capable of setting global norms that every state, however far apart, can be held to. What we are facing is not the end of multilateralism. It is the reminder of its centrality and a moment where it must prove and renew its relevance, and particularly on the environment, which is core of the solution of every challenge, both for human and economic development. So how can multilateralism evolve? That work is already underway with the UN 80 initiative, which reflects a will to make the UN more efficient and better deliver on its mandates. The Pact for the Future points the same way. But as stressed by some, complementary approaches can play a valuable role. Coalition of ambitious, willing states and partnerships bringing together business and civil society do not compete with the multilateral framework. They orbit around it to show what works and often move faster where consensus takes time to build. A prime example of this agile diplomacy lies in the One Planet Summit dynamic launched by the French president, which proved that when the global machinery stalls, an architecture of willing actors can step in, experiment, and ultimately accelerate the pace of the transition. This agile diplomacy also contributed to shape international agreements, such as the Global Biodiversity Framework. I think it can also help us progress on the Global Plastics Treaty, on which a majority of states are willing to start transitioning thanks to harmonized rules. This moment also calls for a leadership that rebuilds trust and favors a logic of genuine partnerships. That was the message delivered by G7 of finance and development ministers under France's presidency. We promoted a new approach to develop financing based on the key tool of country platforms. Country-led global platforms should become the cornerstones of development models. They should be voluntary, aligned with a national whole of government strategy, integrated all environmental component into economic strategy. This is why what we wish to work on with all of you, including for the UN Water Conference, for which France is co-chair of the investment dialogue. Indeed, water is core to all challenges, as there is no dry activity on Earth. But we also need a leadership that is not afraid to own its ambition. Because the environment is not a constraint on sovereignty. It is not a landscape that surrounds us. It is the very reason we exist. We owe it to our people. So, get back to work. Thank you.
Thank you. And I now have pleasure in introducing and calling on Jan Versteeg, of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, the Ambassador and Climate Envoy.

Thank you. Thank you very much, Presidents, Ministers, also for getting us here together. As the Climate Envoy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, I represent a group of four small, not very mountainous countries, one of which is located in the European Union, and three of them are small islands in the Caribbean. And we're all four very fond of multilateralism. And be assured, I won't claim four times three minutes speaking time. We meet at a time when confidence in multilateralism is being tested, as some of the other speakers have put already. Geopolitical tensions are rising. Science is put in doubt. Resources are constrained. And citizens want, as State Secretary Bolesta just pointed out, they want concrete, tangible results. But this is precisely why environmental multilateralism and improving that matters. Environmental challenges do not stop at borders, and no country can address them alone. Environmental cooperation therefore provides a practical test, but also an opportunity to prove that multilateralism can continue to deliver. We need ambition, implementation and delivery. We have seen already that multilateralism can deliver. The Paris Agreement, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and the BBNJ Agreement all demonstrate that countries can come together to establish common goals, frameworks, and rules for shared challenges. At the same time, these experiences also show that multilateral negotiations do not have to be the only pathway for building political momentum and advancing solutions. Coalitions of countries that are ready to move forward can develop common positions, test approaches, build ambition, and create momentum that can feed into and inspire broader multilateral processes. This is complementary to, rather than a replacement for, multilateralism. The inclusive multilateral process remains essential for building legitimacy, finding common ground, and agreeing solutions in the end that can be supported and implemented broadly. The example of plastic negotiations was already mentioned. Another example was Santa Marta, where Colombia and the Netherlands brought 57 countries together for this first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels. The idea was to create a safe space open to all interested states and other stakeholders to discuss solutions and the dilemmas around them departing from this common goal, but also within the boundaries of what we had agreed already at the multilateral level at COP 28 in Dubai years before that. This was not about forming a front against other groups of countries. It is about trying to find solutions acceptable for all in an open and transparent manner. We think such initiatives can build political momentum and support progress in the broader multilateral agenda. And we are confident that Ireland and Tuvalu will bring this process further and be the next pair of co-hosts in what hopefully will be a long series. So the choice, Mr. Chairman, is not between multilateralism and coalitions. We need both. Inclusive multilateral negotiations as the foundation, complemented by coalitions and other initiatives that can build ambition, develop solutions, and accelerate action. Ultimately, the political test is whether these approaches strengthen our ability to deliver. Ambition must lead to implementation, implementation to results, and results to renewed confidence in our international cooperation that is essential. That is how we can strengthen environmental multilateralism and demonstrate its continued relevance for people and the planet. I thank you.

Thank you. We will now hear a series of perspectives from beyond government. And I invite each speaker to share their view, their views on what is needed to strengthen international cooperation and ensure that multilateral processes deliver meaningful outcomes for people and the environment. I invite each speaker to keep their remarks to two minutes. I excuse myself because I have to leave, but I leave you in better hands, which is in the hands of my, my, of Mary Robinson. And I say goodbye by giving the floor to a very dear friend, friend of both chairs of Mary and myself, Hindu Ibrahim. She's the chair of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, and she's also the chair of the group that we both are part of the Planetary Guardians. Indu, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, President, and thank you, Panama, Tuvalu, for the invitation. And Mary and President Santos are really the right person who can help us through this. Let me start by saying that multilateralism must evolve. Most of the state governments are failing. I have been so disappointed by government that using the principles of consensus to block decision, to block what is matter for people, to reject it completely. But I never get failed by the people, by the communities. And this is the best example of the multilateralism. Of course, the world needs multilateralism more than ever. Climate, biodiversity loss, land degradation, pollutions, they do not know border. They are beyond national jurisdictions. As President Santos and Mary said, this is the report we launched yesterday. It's the planetary health check. It's showing us the nine boundary, seven out of them are in danger. Are we ready to sacrifice our life? So multilateralism must remain legitimate. And for that, it must bring not only government, but the peoples who are impacted that can change the decision. And it must give the legal right to nature. If we do not respect the rivers, the mountain, the glaciers, we do not respect ourselves. We will be abusing them. Indigenous peoples are the guardian of all that. And we cannot be only participant. I have my brothers and sisters here in the room. We are right holders. We are knowledge holders. And our knowledge and right must be protected. We must ask questions in multilateralism. Whose knowledge are bringing in the tables? Whose voice are shaping the solutions? So Indigenous people's knowledge can help us to shape the multilateralism. to drive the consensus is not only one country can block. It is if you do not agree, you allow the majority to move. We need the multilateralism that can move the decision to the implementation. And one of the biggest challenge is lacking the international commitment to be turned into the real action. Let me give you a simple example in chat with my organization. We bring communities, elders, women, scientists, local authorities together to map territories, to identify resources, and it's helped us to check solutions to the action, to build resilience to the communities. But of course, pre-lateralism approach can help if there is strength rather than replace multilateralism. So different countries and actors must all speak to a momentum. But those approach must remain transparent, connected, wild in all the system. Let me conclude by saying, for me, remaining environmental multilateralism mean how we can redefine trust. Trust between countries, trust between science and indigenous people's knowledge, trust between government and communities, and trust that international decision will actually improve people's lives. Let us build a multilateralism that is not only more flexible and fast, but more inclusive, more accountable, and more connected to the realities of the peoples on the ground in the territories, who can give holistic visions of all the species. Because if we did a right way multilateralism, of course, we will have the report that cannot take us seven out of the nine, but who can get us back to the safe area we need for our generation, but also for the upcoming generation. We are ready to build it together. But I want to stay, to listen, to do not speak and leave, to stay in the room. Thank you.
Thank you, Hindu, for your passion and commitment, as always. I invite Xanana, Kalvilo, indigenous youth and women leader to offer their perspective.

Thank you. Hi, my name is Xanenin. I come from the cactus forest ecosystem in Puebla. To us, the protection of nature, water, and all forms of life is inherently the protection of our own life, of the stories of our ancestors, of the spiritual forces that keep this world moving. Our peoples have been defenders more than I have been alive, from the very first threats to our waters 500 years ago and until each and every one of us can access water without being sued or killed by a corporation for theft. So just as our relatives from the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, we also believe that our territory is our origin, the source of life we all depend on. And we believe that all references to our ancestral and spiritual territories need to go beyond the inspiration to do the right thing and towards a real commitment to the people, to the plants, animals, hills or streams that call those territories home. After all that has changed already, after all that has been lost so far, I could talk from the fear that I feel every time that I call for rainfall when planting in the fields. Or I could talk about the pain that I have for not knowing the extension of the green and blue that we have lost. Things that I never got to live and that I only know from the memories of my parents. I could talk hours from that. Trend says that actually it helps sense the urgency to mobilize better than hopeful speech. But this time, I want to trust that you're here for a reason, because you already know how hard things are out there. And you know, and you are committed to mobilize all that is in your hands to make a difference. Young people no longer trust our governments or these institutions, but we wish we could. I have learned to believe more in the people that make those institutions, because from a lot of you in the room today, I have seen that you care. And I wish to believe that you have the heart in the right place. I believe in cooperation because every time in history that people have come together to stand against those posing a threat, change is inevitable. I believe in solidarity because when law does not make justice, people do. I believe in other systems because they are here today. Because where I come from, they are taking root and growing stronger every day. And I believe they can teach here more on how multilateralism can work, not in opposition, but in cooperation to the land. All of us are here today because Indigenous peoples once shared that knowledge and science on how to live on this very land. And I believe we can share that again if there is openness to learn. I need to express our concern and disappointment as indigenous peoples, as we have been experiencing a systematic exclusion in international negotiations that decide over our territories, such as the intercessional meetings happening to develop an international legally binding instrument to tackle plastic pollution. Our governments Subject to the people that are obliged to represent, need to uphold the obligations to which they, as member states, adhere at these international spaces, not only in these rooms, but mainly when they go back home, when the people in your countries show up in the streets and in the councils and get together to demand something that's just. In order to create what we dream can be possible to achieve as a true organization of the peoples of the world, we need an effective participation of Indigenous peoples. I believe our multilateralism can become what we want it to become. Imagine what we could do and what we could be capable of if we were to survive an apocalypse. And this is one. How fast could we act to preserve our life if we did not have more time? Because we don't. We stand with the greatest opportunity ahead for the world to demonstrate strong leadership at this critical moment. to stand up for the rights of Indigenous peoples, the planet, the rights of the current and future generations to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment. And we urge you to demonstrate that courage and ambition to secure a successful outcome that meaningfully addresses the global plastic pollution crisis. What happens at the next INC negotiations will haunt us forever, not only in paper, but in our bodies, in our streams, in the ones present here and in futures to come. So as you go over this week and beyond with good intentions in these rooms, I hope that you not forget out there that people are dying, not because the system is not working, but because it is working perfectly. I trust in our abilities to be better as societies, to find ways beyond what it seems to make us different, to dive in the deepest truth that we are here as the same nature.
Thank you. And I invite Rebecca Brown, President and CEO, Center for International Environmental Law, to offer their perspective.

Thank you, Madam Chair, Your Excellencies. I thank Panama and Vanuatu for convening this dialogue. As many have said, multilateralism remains essential to deliver the solutions that the world demands, yet the veto of a few has become its greatest threat, preventing the many from moving forward. A consensus-only decision-making model too often allows short-term interests to override science, equity, and international law. We must replace the power to block with collective incentives to join. The Plastics Treaty is our most immediate test. Success cannot mean agreement at any cost while plastic production remains unchecked and rising. Success will require a legally binding treaty that does not let the hesitation of a few derail progress. Over the last three decades, climate negotiations have shown how a handful of countries use consensus to block decisions on finance and fossil fuels, critical pillars of climate action. That is why the calls for the UNFCCC reform are mounting. and why we need to invest in complementary pathways that enable willing countries to move forward together toward a fossil-free world. The Santa Marta process offers one of these pathways. 57 states shifted the conversation from whether to phase out fossil fuels to how to do so. The next conference, hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland, must focus on the international cooperation countries need to deliver on that transition. including binding legal instruments such as a fossil fuel treaty that can enable countries to jointly overcome the dependence on oil, gas, and coal, the cost of which current wars have laid bare. The coalition of the doers can act together to address public revenue needs, improve energy security, and remove barriers like investor state arbitration. To effectively overcome today's environmental challenges, we must keep human rights and equity at the center of the conversation. real participation of rights holders and civil society, no corporate capture, no false solutions that distract from the urgent progress we need to make. We call on governments to turn this dialogue into coordinated action and deliver an effective plastics treaty, concrete commitments to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels, and a multilateral system that doesn't constrain cooperation, but enables it. The resolution adopting the ICJ's advisory opinion showed the world can move forward, even in the face of objections from a few. This is the moment to show that we have the courage to build the multilateralism future requires and to make it worthy of the trust that we have placed in it. Thank you.
Thank you. And I now give the representative from Uganda an opportunity. He wishes to deliver a few words on behalf of Uganda's candidate for Secretary General. Just one minute, perhaps.

Thank you very much, Madam President. Excellencies, I make these remarks on behalf of Ambassador Olaro Tunnu, Uganda's candidate for Secretary General. I want to thank Panama and Vanuatu for bringing us together. Environmental stewardship by its nature requires much lot of cooperation. In this minute that I have got, I have only four points to leave you with for your consideration. One, rivers, oceans, and the air we breathe connect our countries. Decisions within one country can affect lives and livelihoods far beyond its borders. We need common objectives and national approaches that reflect different needs, priorities, and capacities. Respect for national choices must go hand in hand with responsibility for shared commitments. Cooperation must produce practical results. We can share scientific knowledge, protect shared waters, and strengthen national institutions with technical support for countries that need it. The United Nations can bring countries together and support implementation. Let us judge our cooperation by what we achieve together, and that is cleaner water, productive land, and secure livelihoods for our peoples. Once again, I thank you for organizing this timely event.

Thank you very much.

Thank you. And I now have three more speakers, and then I'm afraid we've had to close the list because of time. But I invite Jane Munk, Scientist Coalition for an Effective Plastics Treaty, to offer their perspective.

Thank you so much, Madam Chair. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for inviting the Scientists' Coalition for an Effective Plastics Treaty to contribute to this important meeting. Let me start with the most important point first. Successful multilateralism needs independent science. This is the basis of objective reality. Governments can make sure that objective reality is the foundation of policy making and importantly, that the assessment of a policy's effectiveness is possible by strengthening the role of independent science in these multilateral environmental processes. This can be achieved by giving independent scientists access to negotiation spaces, having clear rules and procedures that mitigate conflicts of interest, and by upholding transparency as a value. But today, science is being attacked and scientists are being harassed by actors with vested interests. So effective multilateralism should protect the human right to science and also protect the human rights of scientists. At the same time, multilateralism needs to create space for independent science to advise on the best available science and provide input. But oftentimes, multilateral processes lack the mechanisms to integrate independent science, and scientists are oftentimes not given access to negotiation spaces. This substantially limits the effectiveness of multilateral environmental processes. At the Scientists' Coalition for an Effective Plastics Treaty, we self-organized a group of over 450 scientists with expertise on plastic pollution across all life stages. We have been supporting the process to negotiate a global plastics treaty. We are available to all members and observers, and we are committed to supporting the process until we all have a treaty that we can be proud of because it will be effective. And this can only be achieved by grounding it in today's scientific knowledge. We have five key points we'd like to share with you that are prerequisites for an effective plastics treaty. First, independent science is essential for developing an effective treaty, but also for ensuring that the treaty is implemented and that it will lead to ending plastic pollution. Second, a treaty that addresses the full life cycle of plastics with clear obligations will be effective. Third, a treaty that includes provisions on plastics production, managing chemicals of concern, and protecting human health will be effective. Fourth, if the treaty contains legal binding measures, it will be effective. And fifth, a treaty that safeguards against being instrumentalized by vested interests will be effective. We independent scientists stand ready to support you and We also need your support. Science needs friends. Thank you so much.
Thank you very much. And I now call on Ephraim Gomez, Global Policy Impact Director of the World Wildlife Fund International, to offer their perspective.

Thank you, Chair. And above all, thank you to the organizers of this event. We're fully behind you. The best should not be an enemy of the possible in us is an axiom that we often hear, but wrongly, it's applied to the issue, to our ambitions and our commitments, and it should be applied to the company today. Because as we've heard here, the incantation or the arch of consensus bends towards veto today, right? That's very unfortunate, but it's a fact that we have. And if we are serious about a multilateral, environmental multilateralism that actually works, that has impact in the real world, as we just heard from scientists, we cannot be beholden to that logic. It's unfortunate, right? We would've wished for something else, but the point of gravity is not good enough. And it's not even about ambition, it's about being reasonable. I think, for instance, in the plastics negotiation, we hear this, oh, you have high ambitions. It's just reasonable. It's not even super, we're not asking for paradise in these negotiations. So we have three requests in the space of reimagining and refreshing environment for multilateralism. The first is that we discover our agency and feel empowered by this development and the facts that we have on the table. We just put out the report which shows the market shaping effect that we can achieve, for instance, in plastics, if we have a group of first movers, right? And there are many more examples and we will have more and we need to find strength in that. in those developments, including then in plastics and designing a tipping point treaty for plastics. And then our second request is that we actually need to put ourselves into perspective. Consensus is not an iron law. Multilateralism is not singular. We have many different kinds of multilateralisms. And there are ways, our ways and arrangements here can improve, you know, and they must, right, especially if we also envision the kinds of decisions, the arrangements that we need in not only today or yesterday even, but in 5, 10, 15 years, we should be able to recognize it's not good enough. And so third is, of course, that we need to incubate and reform where we can, right? And that's the third request that we have here, is that you leave with a strength and spirit, right, for reform and commitment to action that. Thanks.
Thank you. And the last speaker is Jacob Roghag, co-chair of the Business Coalition for Plastics Treaty, to offer their perspective.

Thank you, Chair, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. My name is Jacob Roghag, and I'm from Tomra. Tomra is a provider of sensor-based solutions for collection and sorting, enabling a circular economy. We have more than 50 years' experience in circular value chains and system in operation in more than 100 countries. I'm speaking today as an industry co-chair for the Business Coalition for a Global Plastic Treaty, representing more than 330 businesses from across the plastic value chain that supports an ambitious and effective global plastic treaty. For businesses, the case of international cooperation is straightforward. Companies operate across borders. Supply chains cross multiple markets. Investment decisions are made for years and often decades into the future.

Yet today, efforts to address plastic.

Pollution are increasingly fragmented, with different rules, definitions, reporting requirements, and policy approaches emerging across jurisdictions. This fragmentation creates uncertainty. It increases compliance costs, complicates investment decisions, and makes it more difficult to scale solutions that can deliver impact across markets. That is why harmonization matters. An effective global plastic treaty can provide a common framework that gives governments the flexibility to implement measures nationally, while at the same time creating enough international alignment to enable businesses to act, invest and innovate with confidence. Businesses are ready to play our part. Across sectors, companies are investing in circular business models, product design, collection recycling system, material innovation and improving transparency across value chains. but business investments alone will not solve this challenge. Governments have a critical role in providing the enabling condition, clear policy direction, common rules, and long-term certainty. These are the foundations to allow innovation to scale and market to respond. The value of a global agreement is not simply that it addresses plastic pollution. It is that it creates and coordinates international response to a shared global challenge, one that helps align markets, unlock investment, and accelerate solution at the pace and scale required. For the business community, that is the opportunity before us, and that is why we continue to support an ambitious, effective, and globally coordinated treaty.
